title: Noise in cities and who has to hear it

turns.speaker: Hector
turns.text: There's a noise map for the city now and you can look up your own street. Mine is well over the level they call harmful.

turns.speaker: Reem
turns.text: Harmful is doing real work in that sentence. It isn't annoyance, it's cardiovascular.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: That's the part people don't believe. Long-term traffic noise tracks with raised blood pressure and heart disease even in people who say it doesn't bother them.

turns.speaker: Hector
turns.text: Even when they're used to it?

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: That's the finding. You habituate consciously. The stress response doesn't habituate, particularly during sleep.

turns.speaker: Reem
turns.text: And it maps onto income almost perfectly. The quiet streets are the expensive ones, everywhere, without exception.

turns.speaker: Hector
turns.text: So it's an environmental inequality that nobody protests about, because you can't see it.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: The cheapest fix is the road surface, oddly. Quieter asphalt takes several decibels off, which is a large change.

turns.speaker: Reem
turns.text: And speed. Noise rises steeply with speed, so twenty limits do more than people expect.

turns.speaker: Hector
turns.text: The electric car point gets overstated, mind you. Above about thirty, it's tyres on road, not the engine.

turns.speaker: Liv
turns.text: Right, so electrification helps in the streets and not on the motorway that the noisiest housing sits beside.

turns.speaker: Reem
turns.text: Which is where barriers would work and almost never get funded.

turns.speaker: Hector
turns.text: Because nobody wins an election on a wall beside a motorway.

points: A city noise map shows many streets above levels classified as harmful.
Long-term traffic noise is linked to raised blood pressure and heart disease, including among people who report not being bothered.
Conscious habituation occurs but the physiological stress response does not, especially during sleep.
Noise exposure maps closely onto income, making it an invisible environmental inequality.
Practical measures include quieter road surfaces and lower speed limits, since noise rises steeply with speed.
Electric vehicles help only below about thirty, as tyre noise dominates above that, leaving motorway-adjacent housing dependent on barriers that are rarely funded.
